questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the one place a business trusts as the accurate, current version of a piece of information is called a ________ of record.
questions.explain: A system of record is the single trusted source for a piece of information. CRM software's whole job is to be that system for every account, contact, and deal, instead of letting the truth scatter across inboxes and spreadsheets.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a Lead and a Contact?
options: A Lead is a single, unqualified record that exists before an account and contact are created; once qualified, it's converted and split into an Account, a Contact, and usually an Opportunity
A Lead is a single, unqualified record that exists before an account and contact are created; once qualified, it's converted into only a Contact, with no Account or Opportunity created
A Lead and a Contact are two names for the exact same record type, used interchangeably depending on the company
A Contact is created first, and gets downgraded into a Lead if a deal later falls through
A Lead can have multiple related Contacts, but a Contact can never be linked back to more than one Lead
Leads exist only for marketing's own tracking and are never visible to a sales rep
questions.explain: A Lead is one messy, unverified record that exists before anyone has decided this is a real account worth pursuing. Converting a qualified Lead splits it into three clean, connected records: an Account, a Contact, and usually an Opportunity — that three-way split is the entire point of conversion.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets the Lead side right but gets conversion wrong on one detail — conversion produces an Account and usually an Opportunity as well, not just a Contact. Dropping the Account and Opportunity from the result is exactly the kind of detail that trips up someone new to this distinction.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a typical lead-to-customer path in the correct order.
items: A lead comes in from a webinar signup or form fill
The lead is qualified and converted into an Account, a Contact, and an Opportunity
The Opportunity moves through sales stages until it closes
The Account and Contact remain in the system permanently, ready for the next opportunity, renewal, or support case
questions.explain: This is the thread that connects first contact to years later: an unqualified lead comes in, gets converted into three clean records once it's worth pursuing, the resulting opportunity is worked through stages to a close, and the account and contact survive that one deal to support everything that happens with the customer afterward.

questions.prompt: Select every metric that's correctly matched to the team responsible for it.
options: Marketing — cost per lead
Sales — win rate
Service — case volume
Marketing — sales cycle length
Sales — customer satisfaction (CSAT)
questions.explain: Cost per lead belongs to marketing, win rate to sales, and case volume to service — each team is judged on the numbers tied to its own stage of the lifecycle. Sales cycle length is a sales metric, not marketing's, and CSAT belongs to service, not sales — both are mismatched in this list.

questions.prompt: A company's lead volume is very high this quarter, but its conversion rate (the share of leads that get qualified and converted) is terrible. What does this combination most likely indicate?
options: Marketing is attracting a large number of the wrong people, rather than sales failing to work the leads it's given
Sales is clearly underperforming, since a high lead volume should guarantee a high conversion rate on its own
The CRM software itself is malfunctioning, since lead volume and conversion rate should always move together
Nothing meaningful can be concluded from lead volume and conversion rate without also knowing the win rate
questions.explain: High lead volume paired with a terrible conversion rate usually points at marketing bringing in the wrong kind of interest, not sales dropping the ball — the lesson's own framing is that a high-volume, low-conversion funnel is a marketing quality problem first.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce's early slogan showed a red circle-and-slash over the word "________," capturing its 1999 pitch of delivering CRM through a browser instead of installed on a company's own servers.
questions.explain: The "No Software" slogan captured Salesforce's founding bet directly: no installation, no hardware to maintain, no IT department required just to get started — radical in 1999, when CRM meant installed software like Siebel Systems.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce cloud to what it's actually built for.
right: Online storefronts, product catalogs, shopping carts, and checkout
Email campaigns and customer journeys that generate and nurture leads
Tracking deals, forecasting revenue, and managing accounts and contacts
A console for working support cases, plus a searchable knowledge base
questions.explain: Sales Cloud is built for tracking deals and pipeline. Service Cloud centers on the case record and gives agents a working console. Marketing Cloud runs campaigns and nurtures leads before sales ever talks to them. Commerce Cloud powers online storefronts and checkout — the two clouds Salesforce grew mainly through acquisition (ExactTarget and Demandware, respectively).

questions.prompt: A company builds an internal app for tracking equipment maintenance — nothing about selling anything. What are they actually building on, and is this "using Sales Cloud differently"?
options: They're building directly on the Salesforce Platform — the underlying database, security model, and customization tools — not customizing Sales Cloud at all
They are using Sales Cloud differently, since every custom build in Salesforce is technically a Sales Cloud configuration
This isn't possible in Salesforce; equipment tracking would require a completely separate piece of software
They're building on Service Cloud, since any non-sales use case defaults to the Service Cloud application
questions.explain: Because the Salesforce Platform is general-purpose, companies build applications on it that have nothing to do with CRM at all — an equipment-maintenance tracker is a new application built directly on the platform, using the same underlying tools Sales Cloud itself was built with. It's not Sales Cloud configured differently; it doesn't touch Sales Cloud at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AppExchange.
options: It launched in 2005, turning Salesforce into a marketplace other companies could build and sell on top of
It lists full applications, components, Lightning data sets, and consultants available to hire
Every listing is free, since AppExchange only distributes Salesforce's own first-party tools
Before installing a listing into a real org, it's worth checking its pricing, data-access requirements, and reviews
Only Salesforce employees are allowed to publish listings on AppExchange
questions.explain: AppExchange launched in 2005 as a marketplace for applications built on the platform, and it lists more than finished apps — components, Lightning data sets, and consultants too. Listings carry real pricing (some free, many paid) and real data-access implications, which is exactly why checking pricing, access, and reviews before installing matters. Listings come from independent companies and developers in the partner ecosystem, not just Salesforce itself.

questions.prompt: A large, complex Salesforce implementation typically touches all four career roles. Put these roles in the order they'd typically engage with a new implementation.
items: Consultant scopes the project and maps business processes onto Salesforce's data model
Architect designs how the data model, security, and integrations fit together
Developer builds the custom logic and integrations the design calls for
Administrator configures and maintains the result for day-to-day use
questions.explain: A typical implementation runs consultant to architect to developer to administrator: the consultant figures out what's needed and maps it to Salesforce's model, the architect designs how the pieces fit together, the developer builds anything point-and-click tools can't, and the administrator maintains the finished org afterward.

questions.prompt: Why can Salesforce push a brand-new feature to millions of users across thousands of companies essentially overnight, with no individual company scheduling an "install the update" IT project?
options: Because of multitenancy — every customer runs on the exact same shared application code and infrastructure, so one platform-wide upgrade reaches everyone at once
Because every customer's Salesforce org is actually a separate installed copy that auto-updates independently on its own schedule
Because Salesforce only ships features to customers who specifically opt into automatic updates ahead of time
Because governor limits force every org to update in lockstep, regardless of the underlying architecture
questions.explain: Multitenancy means every customer — Acme Corp and Globex Inc alike — runs on the identical application code and servers, just with data walled off per tenant. That shared architecture is exactly what lets Salesforce push one platform-wide upgrade and have it reach every tenant simultaneously, instead of each company needing its own scheduled install.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a hard resource cap enforced per transaction — so one tenant's runaway process can't slow down every other tenant sharing the same infrastructure — is called a ________ limit.
questions.explain: Governor limits exist specifically because Salesforce is multitenant: shared infrastructure means the platform has to protect every other tenant from any one tenant hogging resources, so it enforces hard caps on things like queries per transaction and records processed at once.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Salesforce editions and licenses.
options: Enterprise edition gives full access to most automation and customization tools, including Apex and Flow
Developer Edition is a free, full-featured but size-limited edition meant for students and developers to learn and build on
A permission set license grants access to an add-on feature without changing a user's core license
Every user can be assigned more than one user license at the same time, to combine different base access levels
An org's edition has no effect on which features are even available to turn on
questions.explain: Enterprise unlocks most automation and customization tools, including Apex and Flow. Developer Edition is the free, size-limited edition built for learning. A permission set license layers add-on access on top of a user's existing license without replacing it. Every user gets exactly one user license, not several at once — and the edition absolutely determines which features are even available, which is why "what edition are we on?" is one of the first things an admin checks.

questions.prompt: An admin adds a new custom field to the Account object using only Setup's point-and-click tools, with no code written. What did this action actually create, and why does that distinction matter when the field later needs to move from a Sandbox to Production?
options: It created metadata, not data — and moving it to Production means deploying that metadata (the blueprint itself), not copying any business records
It created data, since every new field immediately gets populated with real business values across existing records
It created neither data nor metadata — custom fields exist outside Salesforce's data model entirely until Apex code references them
It created metadata only if the field is later referenced in a Flow; otherwise it behaves as plain data
questions.explain: A field definition is metadata — the blueprint describing the structure, not the business information itself. That's exactly why moving it from Sandbox to Production is a metadata deployment: the new environment gains the structural definition, with no rows of actual business data being copied in the process.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how a Profile and a Permission Set relate to each other?
options: Every user has exactly one Profile, which sets baseline access; Permission Sets are additional, stackable grants layered on top without needing to change the Profile itself
Every user has exactly one Profile, which sets baseline access; assigning any Permission Set replaces that Profile entirely for as long as the Permission Set is active
A Permission Set is simply an older name for what Salesforce now calls a Profile — the two terms describe the same record
Profiles control which specific records a user can see, while Permission Sets control which objects and fields exist in the org
A user can have multiple Profiles active at once, and Salesforce averages their access levels together
Permission Sets are only available to users on the Unlimited edition, never on Enterprise or Developer Edition
questions.explain: Every user has exactly one Profile, setting their baseline access to objects, fields, and apps. Permission Sets are additional, stackable grants layered on top of that Profile, without needing to change or clone it — a user can hold several Permission Sets at once alongside their single Profile.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct "exactly one Profile" detail but gets the stacking wrong — a Permission Set never replaces a user's Profile. It adds on top of it; the Profile keeps functioning as the baseline the whole time a Permission Set is active, which is the one meaningful detail option B inverts.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: using the course's own shorthand, object is the spreadsheet, record is the row, and field is the ________.
questions.explain: Object defines the type of thing being tracked (the spreadsheet), a record is one specific instance of it (a row), and a field is one piece of information captured on that record (a column) — the three-level data model nearly everything in Salesforce comes back to.

questions.prompt: A user switches from the Sales app to the Service app inside the same Salesforce org. What actually changes, and what stays exactly the same?
options: The set of tabs in front of the user changes; their data, their permissions, and which org they're in all stay exactly the same
Their underlying data changes, since each app has its own separate copy of Accounts and Contacts
Their permissions reset to a new baseline, since switching apps is equivalent to switching user profiles
Nothing changes at all — apps in Salesforce are purely cosmetic branding with no effect on the tab bar
questions.explain: An app is just a named, curated bundle of tabs, logo, and color for a particular job function. Switching apps changes which tabs are in front of the user — Sales to Service might mean Opportunities and Leads giving way to Cases and Knowledge — but it never changes the underlying data, the user's permissions, or which org they're logged into.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about list views.
options: A list view is a filtered, sorted table of an object's records, not a dump of every single record
Salesforce ships default list views, like "All Opportunities" or "My Opportunities," out of the box
Only an admin is allowed to create a new list view — regular users can only use ones an admin builds for them
A new list view can be saved privately, just for the creator, or shared with specific user groups
Clicking an object's tab always skips list views entirely and opens one record directly
questions.explain: A list view filters and sorts an object's records rather than dumping everything, Salesforce ships default ones out of the box, and a saved list view can be kept private or shared with specific groups. Both admins and regular users can create their own list views — it isn't admin-only. Clicking an object's tab opens a list view, not a single record.

questions.prompt: At a mid-size HVAC equipment company running on Salesforce, put these events in the order they'd occur, per the course's "day in the life" walkthrough.
items: Marketing runs an email campaign, and everyone who clicks through becomes a Lead
Sales qualifies and converts that Lead into an Account, a Contact, and an Opportunity
The Opportunity moves through stages on the rep's Home page dashboard until it closes
After the sale, a customer's support request becomes a Case worked in a completely different app
Leadership checks a Dashboard built from Reports showing pipeline, win rate, and open case volume
questions.explain: The walkthrough traces one continuous thread: a campaign produces a Lead, sales converts and works it as an Opportunity through to close, service later works a resulting Case in its own app, and leadership finally reviews all of it through Dashboards built on Reports — all pulling from the same underlying Account record the whole way through.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit uses Accounts to represent donor households and Opportunities to represent pledged donations, instead of companies and sales deals. What does this illustrate about the Salesforce platform?
options: The same core objects (Account, Opportunity, and so on) can be adapted to serve very different industries and use cases — this isn't "using Salesforce wrong"
The nonprofit is actually misusing Salesforce, since Accounts and Opportunities are reserved exclusively for for-profit sales processes
This only works because the nonprofit purchased a completely separate product unrelated to standard Salesforce objects
Opportunities must be renamed at the database level before they can represent anything other than a sales deal
questions.explain: The common thread across wildly different organizations — a nonprofit, a university, a small business — is that they're all still built from the same objects, records, and fields, just adapted to what that organization actually tracks. A donor household fits naturally into the Account object, and a pledged donation fits naturally into Opportunity, without needing a different underlying platform at all.
